author: tom
title: How to start playing table tennis as an adult
seo_title: How to start playing table tennis as an adult
description: How adults in England can start playing table tennis: free public tables, club sessions for beginners, what to bring, coaching and joining a local league.
summary: You don't need a bat, a partner or any experience to start. A free public table or a club's social session is enough, and a local league can follow within a season.
key_points: Table Tennis England's table finder maps clubs, outdoor tables, parlours and social sessions near you.
Most clubs lend bats to newcomers, so you need only comfortable sportswear and indoor trainers.
Some clubs run Back to TT sessions for returning adults and Bat & Chat sessions for over-50s.
Club Play membership of Table Tennis England is free. Compete membership, which covers local leagues, is £26 for adults in 2026-27.
Learn a legal serve and the basic rules early: they are the same in a park as in a league.
body: The quickest way to start is to find a table near you on Table Tennis England's table finder, then either play on a free public table with a friend or go along to a club's beginners' or social session. You don't need your own bat at first, you don't need to be fit, and you don't need to have played before.
## Find somewhere to play

Table Tennis England, the governing body for the sport in England, runs an online table finder that maps places to play within a radius you choose, from five to 50 miles. You can filter by type: clubs, outdoor tables, Ping Pong Parlours, community and social hubs, leisure centres, bars and cafes, and sessions for particular groups.

Outdoor tables in parks and public spaces are the easiest start. Many are part of Ping!, Table Tennis England's programme for public tables in parks, shopping centres and community venues. You don't need to be a member, and at many sites you don't need your own equipment either, though bringing a bat and a few balls is safer.
Some leisure centres have tables you can book, which is a good option in winter if you already have someone to play with.
## Go to a club session

A club is where most people improve. Clubs usually cater for all ages and abilities, with some evenings for social play and others for coaching or league matches. Ring or email before you go and ask which session suits a beginner. Most will tell you to bring nothing but yourself.

Two Table Tennis England programmes are aimed at adults and show up as filters on the table finder. Back to TT is a social session for people thinking of returning to the game, mostly aged 25 to 55. Bat & Chat is an organised social session for people over 50. There is also a filter for women and girls' sessions and one for venues with disability access.

At a first session expect a mix of warm-up rallies, simple drills such as forehand to forehand, and some friendly games. Nobody minds if you miss. Watch how other players stand: knees bent, close to the table, bat in front of the body.
## What to bring
Wear comfortable sportswear and indoor trainers with soft, non-marking soles, because sports-hall floors can be slippery and you will move more than you expect. Take a drink.

Most clubs have spare bats. Once you know you'll keep playing, buy a ready-made bat from a specialist table tennis brand rather than a supermarket set, and keep it in a case so the rubbers stay clean. Our guide to [what bat a beginner should buy](/guide/what-table-tennis-bat-to-buy.html) explains what to look for at each stage. Any bat you use in a competition needs one black side and one brightly coloured side, and in Table Tennis England competitions the rubbers must be a brand and type authorised by the International Table Tennis Federation (ITTF).
## Learn the rules early

Club sessions are friendly, but they follow the same laws as the professional game. The ones you will meet in your first week are the serve and the scoring: games go to 11, you need two clear points from 10-10, and the serve changes every two points. Most new players' serves are illegal without them knowing, usually because the ball is held in the fingers or not tossed high enough. Read [what makes a serve legal](/guide/legal-serve-rules.html) and our five-minute guide to the rules and you will be ahead of many club players.
## Get some coaching

A few sessions with a coach early on save months of unlearning bad habits, particularly in the grip and the forehand stroke. Many clubs include coaching in their session fees or run group sessions for improvers. Ask at your club whether a qualified coach is available and whether there are group or one-to-one options.
## Join a league

Once you can keep a rally going and know the rules, a local league is the next step. Leagues are run locally, and those with several divisions let a beginner start against players of a similar standard. Your club will usually enter you in one of its teams.

Local league play is covered by Table Tennis England's Compete membership and above. For 2026-27, Compete costs £26 for adults, £14 for under-19s and is free for under-11s. Compete Plus, which adds national competitions, costs £49 for adults. If you only play socially at a club, Club Play membership is free and includes public liability insurance; there is also a free Supporter membership for fans. Your club or league secretary will tell you which you need.
Our guide to [finding a club and joining a league in England](/guide/find-a-table-tennis-club-england.html) goes through the steps and how your results are counted once you start competing.
## Play at home

If you want to practise between sessions, Table Tennis England has advice on turning a dining table into somewhere to play. It won't bounce like a full-size table, but it is enough to work on your serve and your touch. A full-size table needs a space around it, so measure before you buy one.
## Your next steps

Look up the table finder, pick a session this week and turn up. When you are hooked, read our guides to [the playing styles](/guide/table-tennis-playing-styles.html) and spin to understand what you are learning, and watch how the best do it in the [world rankings](/rankings.html) and the [events calendar](/events/).
